topic: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 vs V4.1 Flash: which one you pull for local hardware
title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash vs V4 Pro 0813: Which Fits Your Machine Tonight
description: Two DeepSeek flagships are sitting on Hugging Face, and the louder one is not the one your machine can hold: the smallest published V4 Pro 0813 file is 850 GB, while the smallest V4.1 Flash 1017 file is 233 GB. DeepSeek's own benchmark table even puts the smaller Flash ahead of the Pro on coding-agent work. You'll learn how mixture-of-experts memory math really works, what SSD streaming buys a home machine, and a one-line rule for picking tonight's download. Subscribe for weekly local-model picks, and drop your setup in the comments. (Narration is AI-generated.)

narration_full: Tonight it's DeepSeek Pro or Flash, and one number decides. You're picking between two DeepSeek downloads tonight. The Pro's smallest published file is eight hundred fifty gigabytes on disk. The Flash's smallest is two hundred thirty-three gigabytes on your drive. Both are quantized, stored at lower precision to shrink the file. One file each. Both ship as a single-file build you can run tonight. Unsloth publishes them on Hugging Face, fully open weights. Each is a mixture of experts, a model that wakes only a slice of itself per word. Those active parameters, the slice that does the work, stay small. Every expert still has to sit on your drive or in your memory. So what fits tonight? Drive streaming, pulling parts of the model from your fast drive into memory when they are needed, is the trick. On Unsloth's numbers, a big Spark-class machine holds the Flash. Nothing published yet holds the Pro. Picture a master carpenter with a rolling tool chest. The daily tools ride inside; the rare ones fetch from the store across the street, your drive. Except a router inside the model picks per word, and the fetch costs seconds instead of a trip across town. Here's the twist. On DeepSeek's own table, the Flash scores ninety point six on the terminal bench, ahead of the Pro. The smaller pull is the quality pick for coding and agents, not the compromise. The Pro still leads the world-knowledge rows, where its bigger backbone earns its keep. And if you ever rent these in DeepSeek's cloud, the Flash is the cheaper seat there too. So tonight: count your free memory. Grab the Unsloth single-file build that fits. Run it in llama dot cpp or Unsloth Desktop. Let your drive hold the overflow. Set reasoning effort to trade speed against depth. The rule to keep: your free memory picks the model. Tonight, it picks the Flash.

notes_for_review: Number budget: exactly three spoken numbers (850 GB, 233 GB, 90.6); every on-screen digit is spoken in the same scene and beat. Because of this, (1) the Pro's Terminal-Bench 2.1 score of 87.9 appears only as an unlabeled shorter bar, and (2) the bench version digit '2.1' is omitted from screen text since it cannot be spoken; verify that showing 'Terminal-Bench' without the version is acceptable rather than misleading. 'Big Spark-class machine' stands in for Unsloth's 128GB+ RAM figure, which was outside the spoken-number budget. 'Nothing published yet holds the Pro' hedges against Unsloth's still-filling Pro GGUF repo. No tokens-per-second, MLX, or Ollama-local claims are made, per the unverified list. TTS check: 'llama dot cpp' should read as llama.cpp; adjust spelling if the voice mangles 'cpp'. All scenes avoid ALL-CAPS narration tokens (GGUF/SSD appear on screen only), no em dashes, no hype words, and only one 'not X' antithesis (s07).
